hook.text: One processor. A keyboard, a disk, a screen, and a crowd of programs that all want it, right now.

who.text: Someone has to decide who gets what. That someone is the operating system.

alloc.text: It is a resource allocator: it shares out the CPU, the memory and the devices.

control.text: And it is a control program: it stops errors and improper use.

kernel.text: Its core is the kernel, the one program that runs the whole time the computer is on.

keyQ.text: First puzzle. You press a key. How does the CPU find out?

poll.text: One way is polling. The CPU keeps asking the keyboard: done yet? Done yet?

pollBad.text: Almost every answer is no, and every question is wasted work.

irq.text: The better way is an interrupt. The CPU gets on with real work. When the device finishes, its controller taps the CPU on the shoulder.

s1.text: The CPU finishes the instruction it is on, and saves the program counter and the registers.

s2.text: It looks up the interrupt vector to find the right handler, and runs that interrupt service routine.

s3.text: Then it puts back what it saved, and carries on exactly where it stopped.

trap.text: A trap is the software version: an interrupt caused by a program, for a request, or an error like division by zero.

dmaQ.text: Now the disk. It sends megabytes. One interrupt for every word would bury the CPU.

dma.text: So it uses D M A, direct memory access. The device controller copies a whole block straight into memory, without the CPU.

dma2.text: And it interrupts once, when the block is done. One interrupt per block, not per word.

modeQ.text: Last puzzle. What stops a program from simply taking over the machine?

mode.text: The hardware does. One mode bit. One means user mode. Zero means kernel mode.

priv.text: Privileged instructions, like talking to devices or setting the timer, only run in kernel mode. Try one in user mode, and the CPU refuses.

door.text: The only way in is a controlled door: a system call, a trap, or an interrupt. On the way out, the bit goes back to one.

loop.text: And a program that just loops forever, never asking for anything?

timer.text: Before handing over the CPU, the OS sets a hardware timer. When it runs out, it interrupts, and the OS is back in control.

ex1.text: The OS allocates resources and controls their use.

ex3.text: D M A: one interrupt per block.

ex4.text: Mode bit: one is user, zero is kernel.

ex5.text: The timer always gives control back.
